A robust deep learning framework for RNA 
5‑methyluridine modification prediction using 
integrated features
Naif Almusallam1, Salman Khan2, Fawaz Khaled Alarfaj1 and Nijad Ahmad3* 
Abstract 
Background  The discovery of RNA 5-methyluridine (m5U) modifications is vital in computational biology due 
to their essential significance in different biological processes. This study presents a powerful predictor named 
5-meth-Uri, which improves the overall accuracy of m5U modification predictions. The proposed method combines 
a composite of dinucleotide and trinucleotide-based auto-cross covariance with six physicochemical parameters 
to generate a feature vector. We select essential features using an unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) 
technique to enhance the model’s efficiency. Finally, an intelligent computation Deep Neural Network (DNN) was uti-
lized to classify RNA 5-methyluridine (m5U).
Results  The model’s performance was evaluated on two benchmark datasets, namely mature mRNA and full tran-
script, using tenfold cross-validation and an independent test. The proposed model achieved an average accuracy 
of 95.13% and 97.36% on the training set and 95.73% and 96.51% on the independent test sets for the full transcript 
and mature mRNA datasets, respectively. 5-meth-Uri demonstrated around 7.15% and 3.98% higher accuracy on train-
ing data and 5.42% and 3.52% higher accuracy on independent samples for both datasets compared to existing 
models.
Conclusions  Its high accuracy and reliability make 5-meth-Uri a promising tool for researchers with potential bio-
medical and pharmaceutical applications.
Keywords  DACC​, TACC​, PCA, Deep learning, RNA 5-methyluridine
Background
Revealing approximately 170 cellular RNA chemical 
alterations [1, 2], RNA mapping tools have significantly 
advanced the study of RNA epigenetic changes. Among 
them are well-known signs such as 5-methylcytosine 
(m5C), N6-methyladenosine (m6A), and pseudou-
ridine (Ψ), as well as less investigated changes includ-
ing 7-methylguanosine (m7G) and dihydrouridine (D). 
RNA changes affect all four bases: uracil (U), guanine 
(G), cytosine (C), and adenine (A), as well as the ribose 
sugar [3]. tRNA and rRNA are the most highly altered 
species. These chemical alterations are crucial for pro-
tein synthesis, gene expression, and modifications to 
RNA-modifying enzymes [4]. While every method has 
restrictions in sequence context and modification speci-
ficity [5], more advanced recognition techniques, such 
as liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC–MS)

[6] and next-generation sequencing (NGS), have enabled 
researchers to study these modifications more compre-
hensively [6].
Among these modifications, 5-methyluridine (m5U) 
stands out for its biological significance. 5-methyluri-
dine (m5U) is primarily found in non-coding RNAs and 
transfer RNAs (tRNAs), such as ribosomal RNA (rRNA) 
and messenger RNA (mRNA) [7]. m5U modifications 
are catalyzed by enzymes such as TrmA in bacteria and 
TRMT2A in humans. This modification contributes to 
RNA stability and structure, particularly in the conserved 
T-loop motif. However, despite its prevalence, the biolog-
ical functions and mechanisms of m5U remain underex-
plored. Research [8, 9] has connected m5U to processes 
like stress response, plant development, disorders includ-
ing lupus and breast cancer, and stress response. Though 
frequently costly and providing limited data owing to 
technological difficulties, experimental approaches such 
as miCLIP-Seq [10, 11] and iCLIP [9] offer insightful 
analysis. Advancement of our knowledge of m5U sites in 
health and illness depends on the development of strong 
computational approaches to precisely identify them. 
To address the challenges in spotting RNA modifica-
tions [12–14], researchers have suggested using Machine 
Learning (ML) methods.
The experimental identification of all RNA changes 
is costly and complex, leading to the widespread use of 
computational approaches. Numerous machine learn-
ing-based techniques have been created to forecast 
RNA changes, i.e., RNA modification [15], ConsRM 
[16], iRNA-Methyl [17], SRAMP [18], WHISTLE [19], 
DirectRMDB [20], MODOMICS [21], m7GHub V2.0 
[22], m5C site predictors (RNADSN [23], iRNA-m5C 
[24]), and pseudouridine predictors (RNAm5Cfinder 
[25], PPUS [26], and iRNA-PseU [27]). To enhance the 
detection of m5U-modified sites, a limited number of 
experimental and computational methods have been 
developed to handle the complexity of RNA modifica-
tions [28, 29]. Among them, m5UPred, created by Jiang 
et al. [30], uses a support vector machine method using 
sequence-derived characteristics. For mature mRNA, the 
suggested model achieved an accuracy of 89.91%, and for 
full transcripts, 83.60%. Based on an SVM classifier, Ao 
et  al. [31] introduced the m5U-SVM model using ten-
fold cross-validation. The m5U-SVM achieved accuracies 
of 94.36% for mature mRNA and 88.88% for full tran-
scripts. Both models have yielded promising results in 
terms of accuracy; however, these models are developed 
based on conventional learning methods, which are una-
ble to accurately predict the m5U sites due to the high 
similarity between m5U and non-m5U sites. In addi-
tion, these models require substantial amounts of human 
expertise and capability to extract prominent features 
automatically. Recently, Noor et  al. [32] proposed a 
computational method that leverages pseudo-k-tuple 
nucleotide compositions as a feature extraction method, 
enriching them with structural and sequence-order fea-
tures and refining feature selection using SHAP to retain 
the most discriminative attributes. The proposed model 
achieved 91.47% and 95.86% accuracy, surpassing exist-
ing predictors for accurately identifying RNA’s 5-methy-
luridine (m5U) modifications on the same benchmark 
datasets. However, these models may struggle to capture 
deeper contextual relationships within RNA sequences 
and often lack integration with complementary encoding 
strategies, which can limit the overall performance and 
generalizability of the trained models.
This study introduces a computational predictor to 
accurately identify 5-methyluridine (m5U) modifica-
tions, utilizing efficient feature extraction methods. 
Firstly, the proposed model uses a composite feature 
extraction algorithm, i.e., Dinucleotide-based Auto-Cross 
Covariance (DACC) and Trinucleotide-based auto-Cross 
Covariance (TACC), to convert an RNA sequence into 
a feature vector. The DACC combines Dinucleotide-
based Auto-Covariance (DAC) and Dinucleotide-based 
Cross-Covariance (DCC). Similarly, TACC combines 
Trinucleotide-based Auto Covariance (TAC) and Trinu-
cleotide-based Cross-Covariance (TCC). Through this 
integration process, we develop new composite feature 
vectors that enable the model to represent biomedical 
information more effectively. Principal Component Anal-
ysis (PCA) was employed as a feature selection method 
to enhance these feature vectors further and select the 
discriminative ones by removing noisy and irrelevant 
features. Moreover, a Deep Neural Network (DNN) was 
used to classify and accurately identify 5-methyluridine 
(m5U) modifications through a tenfold cross-validation. 
The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed 
model outperforms existing prediction models on both 
datasets in terms of accuracy and other performance 
measurement parameters. The proposed model achieved 
95.13% and 97.36% training accuracy, as well as 95.73% 
and 96.51% on independent test samples from both data-
sets (Fig. 1).
Results and discussion
Experimental setup
To experiment, we use an Intel Core i7, which is suitable 
for desk work and basic computing, paired with a 256 GB 
SSD for faster booting, reading, and writing than HDDs. 
The system includes 16 GB RAM, enabling smooth multi-
tasking. Pre-installed Python 3 libraries, such as NumPy, 
SciPy, TensorFlow, Keras, Pandas, and Matplotlib, sup-
port data science workflows, including machine learning 
(ML) model training and data analysis. This setup is ideal

Analysis of nucleotide composition
In this section, we used Two-Sample Logo software [33] 
to analyze nucleotide composition differences between 
sequences with and without m5U modifications. This 
method highlighted significant residue enrichment or 
depletion at m5U-modified sites (Fig. 2). Statistical anal-
ysis using a t-test (p < 0.05) revealed distinct patterns in 
both modes. In the full transcript mode, sequences dis-
played an enrichment of G at locations − 3 (ratio: 50) 
and − 8 (ratio: 35), U at location 1, and C at locations 7 
and 8. Similarly, the mature mRNA mode showed nota-
ble enrichment of G at − 8 and − 3, while C clustered 
around positions 6–9. Homopolymeric regions, such as 
G (− 10 to − 8) and C (6 to 9), were observed. Addition-
ally, sequence-specific differences emerged: G was more 
concentrated in the Mature mRNA mode, whereas C 
was enriched at location 19 in the full transcript mode. 
Notably, when C was at position − 1, the mature mRNA 
mode showed a higher concentration of G, while the full 
transcript mode enriched for A. These findings suggest 
that nucleotide composition and enrichment patterns 
can be reliable indicators for predicting m5U modifica-
tion sites in RNA.

Hyperparameters and optimizations
This section focuses on optimizing hyperparameters 
using a grid search technique for the DNN model to 
evaluate performance across various configurations. 
Key stochastic parameters assessed were the number 
of iterations, activation function, and learning rate. 
Firstly, we conducted several experiments to examine 
the activation function outcomes (i.e., ReLU, Sigmoid, 
and Tanh) and learning rates (ranging from 0.001 to 
0.1). The grid search outcomes revealed that the DNN 
classifier achieved a maximum accuracy of 97.36% on 
the mature mRNA dataset and 95.13% on the full tran-
script dataset, using the Tanh activation function and a 
learning rate of 0.01. The optimal configuration is sum-
marized in Table 1.
Moreover, experiments were conducted to assess the 
performance of the DNN model by varying the number 
of training epochs. The error loss steadily decreased with 
increasing epochs. For instance, in the full transcript 
dataset (Fig.  3A), error loss dropped from 1.143 at the 
first epoch to 0.002 by the 50th epoch. Similarly, for the 
mature mRNA dataset (Fig. 3B), the error rate reduced 
from 1.57 to 0.003 after 50 epochs. These findings indi-
cate that 50 epochs are optimal for both datasets, as error 
rates stabilize at this point.
Performance analysis
This section analyzes the performance of the proposed 
model on both datasets, using both individual and com-
posite features, before and after feature selection, and 
evaluates it through tenfold cross-validation (CV). The 
mean CV results were calculated by repeating the strati-
fied loop process 100 times, ensuring robust and reli-
able outcomes by randomly distributing the training data 
across folds. Table  2 presents results for the full tran-
script dataset, showing that combining features yielded 
better outcomes than individual feature methods. For 
example, using TACC (a composite of TAC and TCC), 
the DNN achieved 92.42% accuracy and a Matthews cor-
relation coefficient (MCC) of 0.834. Similarly, DACC (a 
composite of DAC and DCC) resulted in 92.56% accu-
racy and an MCC of 0.837. Combining DACC and TACC 
further improved accuracy to 93.59% and MCC to 0.860. 
Applying feature selection to reduce the dimensionality 
of the composite feature vector enhanced overall perfor-
mance, with the DNN achieving 95.13% accuracy and an 
MCC of 0.894.

Similarly, the model’s performance was assessed on the 
mature mRNA dataset using various sequence formula-
tion methods, as shown in Table 3. The results demon-
strated superior performance with composite features 
compared to individual methods. For instance, using 
composite features DACC + TACC, the model achieved 
an accuracy of 95.93%, with a specificity of 96.14%, a sen-
sitivity of 95.73%, and an MCC of 0.919. Applying feature 
selection to reduce hybrid feature dimensionality fur-
ther improved performance, increasing the accuracy to 
97.36%, specificity to 97.56%, sensitivity to 97.15%, and 
MCC to 0.947.
Moreover, the model’s performance was evaluated 
using the area under the curve (AUC) metric, a meas-
ure of the accuracy of binary classifiers, where higher 
values indicate improved performance. The proposed 
model achieved AUC values of 0.982 and 0.992 on the 
full transcript and mature mRNA datasets, respectively, 
leveraging an efficient feature set (Fig.  4). These out-
comes validate the superior predictive capabilities of the 
proposed model, particularly when utilizing the 10-fold 
cross-validation approach and the selected features.
Similarly, to assess how well the extracted features dis-
tinguish between target classes, we applied t-distributed 
stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) for data visu-
alization. This technique projects the high-dimensional 
feature vectors into a two-dimensional space for intuitive 
inspection (Fig. 5). We conducted this analysis on both 
the full transcript and mature mRNA datasets, compar-
ing feature distributions before and after dimensional-
ity reduction using composite features. Before feature 
selection, the data exhibited significant overlap between 
classes, indicating limited discriminative power. After 
applying PCA to select the most informative features, the 
resulting visualizations revealed more apparent class sep-
aration. This improved distinction highlights the effec-
tiveness of the selected features in reducing complexity 
while enhancing the model’s ability to differentiate m5U 
sites from non-m5U sequences.

bor (KNN) [37], and support vector machine (SVM) 
[38]. All machine learning classifiers were subjected to 
thorough hyper-parameter tuning using a grid search 
strategy combined with 10-fold cross-validation to 
ensure fair and optimal performance comparisons with 
the proposed model. Table  4 compares the proposed

Conclusions
With 5-methyluridine (m5U) being particularly impor-
tant post-transcriptionally, RNA modification plays a 
vital role in determining disease development and con-
trolling biological activities. Understanding RNA func-
tion and its connections to disease depends on this 
change marked by methylation at the C5 site of uridine. 
To facilitate the precise identification of m5U sites, we 
present a novel 5-meth-Uri model based on deep learn-
ing, designed to leverage hybrid feature integration and 
rigorous evaluation through tenfold cross-validation and 
independent datasets. The 5-meth-Uri model addresses 
challenges such as overfitting by employing optimized 
hyperparameter tuning and feature selection techniques. 
It demonstrated exceptional performance, achieving 
95.13% and 97.36% accuracy on both datasets, respec-
tively, while maintaining robust accuracy levels of 95.73% 
and 96.51% on independent test datasets. These results 
significantly surpass conventional machine learning 
models and other state-of-the-art prediction methods. 
With its superior accuracy and reliability, 5-meth-Uri 
is poised to enhance research into RNA modifications 
and their biological roles, particularly in stress response 
mechanisms and disease pathogenesis, including breast 
cancer. Moreover, this model holds promise for aiding 
the development of therapeutic strategies targeting RNA 
modifications, paving the way for innovations in biomed-
ical research and personalized medicine.
In the future, we plan to develop a user-friendly online 
web platform for the proposed 5-meth-Uri model, ena-
bling biologists to access and utilize it for convenient 
prediction of RNA 5-methyluridine modifications. Addi-
tionally, we aim to explore advanced parallel deep-learn-
ing models[4, 40, 41] to enhance computational efficiency 
and accuracy.

Reliable machine-learning models and validation of ML 
approaches depend on datasets. This work made use of 
the full transcript and mature mRNA databases, previ-

sample, a 41-nt modified sequence with an experimen-
tally identified U-site was produced; however, unmodi-

and 80% was used for training. The full transcript dataset, 
for example, contained 1534 positive and 2862 negative 
training samples. Similarly, 983 positive and 985 nega-
tive training samples were utilized for the mature mRNA 
dataset. Furthermore, for the independent test set, the

have been used in this work: Trinucleotide-based Auto-
Cross Covariance (TACC) and Dinucleotide-based Auto-
Cross Covariance (DACC). Dinucleotide-based auto 
covariance (DAC) and Dinucleotide-based Cross Covari-
ance (DCC) are combined by DACC. TACC combines 
trinucleotide-based cross-covariance (TCC) with trinu-
cleotide-based auto-covariance (TAC). Consequently, 
where N is the number of physicochemical indices (i.e.,

arated by lag nucleic acids along the sequence, as math-
ematically expressed in Eqs. (3–4), respectively.

PCA features selection
In statistical machine learning, feature vectors play 
a crucial role in making predictions. However, high-
dimensional feature spaces can negatively impact 
model accuracy due to the presence of irrelevant, 
redundant, and noisy features. Additionally, such mod-
els require significantly more computational resources 
and memory for training and testing. Various feature 
selection methods have been developed to reduce the 
feature space by eliminating unnecessary features, 
thereby addressing these challenges and enhancing 
predictive performance. PCA is a widely used multi-
variate technique that transforms correlated features 
into a smaller set of uncorrelated ones, known as prin-
cipal components. The primary objective of PCA is to 
reduce the dimensionality of feature vectors while pre-
serving critical discriminative features. In this study, 
we employed Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to 
reduce the original 144-dimensional feature space (as 
shown in Table 8) while preserving the most informa-
tive components. We gradually applied PCA, starting 
from the complete feature set and incrementally reduc-
ing the dimensions, evaluating model performance at 
each step (Fig. 6 A, B). The proposed model achieved 
the best performance using 80 principal components

Deep neural network architecture
Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are a type of machine 
learning model designed to inspire how the human brain 
processes information. The DNN structure consists of an 
input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. 
The hidden layers play a crucial role in recognizing features 
and patterns within the data that aren’t immediately obvi-
ous. Adding more hidden layers can improve the model’s 
ability to handle complex patterns, but it also makes the 
network more difficult to train, more resource-intensive, 
and prone to overfitting. One of the primary benefits of 
DNNs is their ability to automatically extract features from 
data, eliminating the need for manual feature engineering. 
They can learn directly from raw, unlabeled, or unstruc-
tured data using standard training methods, as noted in 
[47]. Due to their depth and flexibility, Deep Neural Net-
works (DNNs) outperform traditional machine learning 
methods in complex classification tasks. They are widely 
applied in fields such as bioengineering [40], natural lan-
guage processing [34], image recognition [35], and speech 
recognition, demonstrating their versatility and effective-
ness across various domains.

Although the DNN model exhibited promising results, 
several limitations are associated with the model: (a) the 
model is sensitive to the number of neurons in the hid-
den layers; i.e., a few neurons may cause underfitting 
problems, whereas too many neurons may contribute to 
overfitting issues. (b) In general, a network with more 
hidden layers in a training or testing process can lead to 
better accuracy; however, it also raises significant issues, 
such as increased computation cost, complexity, and van-
ishing gradients. (c) Due to its high computational com-
plexity, the model required high-performance computing 
to generate reasonable results within a reasonable time. 
To address these issues, we applied several techniques. 
For example, a dropout technique was employed at each 
hidden layer to overcome the issue of overfitting [51–53]. 
Similarly, a balanced number of hidden layers (i.e., four 
hidden layers) was configured in the network to over-
come the computational complexity and vanishing gradi-
ent issue [54, 55].
Evaluation of performance
Performance indicators are crucial for assessing the reli-
ability of a machine-learning model. Accuracy (ACC) 
assesses overall precision by dividing the number of cor-
rectly classified instances (true positives and true nega-
tives) by the total number of cases, providing a measure 
of the model’s effectiveness. Sensitivity (SN), also known 
as recall, measures the model’s ability to accurately 
identify positive instances. Specificity (SP) measures 
the correct identification of negative cases. Matthews

Abstract: Background The discovery of RNA 5-methyluridine (m5U) modifications is vital in computational biology due to their essential significance in different biological processes. This study presents a powerful predictor named 5-meth-Uri, which improves the overall accuracy of m5U modification predictions. The proposed method combines a composite of dinucleotide and trinucleotide-based auto-cross covariance with six physicochemical parameters to generate a feature vector. We select essential features using an unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) technique to enhance the model’s efficiency. Finally, an intelligent computation Deep Neural Network (DNN) was uti- lized to classify RNA 5-methyluridine (m5U). Results The model’s performance was evaluated on two benchmark datasets, namely mature mRNA and full tran- script, using tenfold cross-validation and an independent test. The proposed model achieved an average accuracy of 95.13% and 97.36% on the training set and 95.73% and 96.51% on the independent test sets for the full transcript and mature mRNA datasets, respectively. 5-meth-Uri demonstrated around 7.15% and 3.98% higher accuracy on train- ing data and 5.42% and 3.52% higher accuracy on independent samples for both datasets compared to existing models. Conclusions Its high accuracy and reliability make 5-meth-Uri a promising tool for researchers with potential bio- medical and pharmaceutical applications.
